package_info.package_manager: N/A (exploits Atlassian Confluence via CVE-2023-22527, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.package_versions: Confluence Data Center and Server (affected versions prior to January 2024 patch)
package_info.why_malicious: The Godzilla backdoor is a fileless, in-memory malware that exploits a critical template injection vulnerability (CVE-2023-22527) in Atlassian Confluence. It enables unauthenticated remote code execution, persistent in-memory webshell access, and AES-encrypted C2 communication, all while evading traditional file-based detection.

execution_context.trigger: HTTP POST request to vulnerable template endpoint

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At HTTP request-time, the attacker injects OGNL/JavaScript code via a template parameter, which is evaluated by the vulnerable Confluence server, enabling arbitrary code execution and loading of a Base64-encoded Java class (webshell) into memory.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Template injection with arbitrary code execution is a hallmark of exploitation, especially when it loads encoded payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Templates should only render data, not execute attacker-supplied code or load arbitrary classes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; dynamic code execution via user input is never legitimate in this context.
key_indicators: OGNL/JavaScript code injection in HTTP POST
Use of ScriptEngineManager for dynamic code execution

execution_context.trigger: In-memory class loading after template injection

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the injected class uses Java reflection to access private fields and Tomcat internals, then injects a custom Valve into the Tomcat pipeline, establishing a persistent in-memory webshell.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Reflection to access private fields and inject custom Valves is highly abnormal and enables deep server compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Application code should not manipulate servlet container internals or inject runtime webshells.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Reflection is used in frameworks, but not for arbitrary field access or webshell injection.
key_indicators: Injection of custom Valve into Tomcat

execution_context.trigger: Webshell command execution via HTTP requests

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the in-memory webshell receives AES-encrypted commands via HTTP, decrypts and executes them on the server, then encrypts and returns the output to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: AES-encrypted command-and-control over HTTP is a strong indicator of a backdoor.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Servlet Valves should not process arbitrary encrypted commands or execute system commands.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Encryption for legitimate API traffic, but not for command execution.

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a malicious HTTP POST exploiting CVE-2023-22527 to inject OGNL/JavaScript code and a Base64-encoded payload.
attack_chain.leads_to: In-memory loading and execution of the Godzilla webshell class.

attack_chain.action: Injected code decodes and loads the MemGodValueShell class into JVM memory using reflection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Injection of a custom Valve into the Tomcat pipeline.

attack_chain.action: Custom Valve (GodzillaValue) is activated, establishing a persistent in-memory webshell.
attack_chain.leads_to: Server is now backdoored and awaits attacker commands.

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends AES-encrypted commands via HTTP to the webshell, which decrypts, executes, and returns encrypted results.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control of the server and exfiltration of results.

behavioral_signatures: Template injection leading to dynamic class loading
Injection of custom Valve objects at runtime
file_indicators: No persistent files (fileless); suspicious in-memory Valve objects
Unusual classes loaded in JVM memory (e.g., MemGodValueShell, GodzillaValue)
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to /template/aui/text-inline.vm with OGNL/JavaScript payloads
AES-encrypted HTTP traffic to Confluence endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for template injection attempts and OGNL/JavaScript code in HTTP POST requests to Confluence endpoints. Detect in-memory anomalies such as unexpected Valve objects or classes loaded via reflection. Look for AES-encrypted command patterns in HTTP traffic. Use memory forensics to identify webshells that do not exist on disk. Correlate with known C2 patterns for Godzilla and similar backdoors.
